title: Shouldn’t teachers…teach?
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien argues that teacher preparation spent thirty years training teachers to facilitate rather than instruct, leaving two generations without the craft of explaining, modelling, checking understanding and giving timely feedback. He contrasts teaching with medicine, trades, sport and music, where technique is taught explicitly before improvisation. He marshals Rosenshine, Willingham and the science of reading to claim the evidence has long favoured explicit instruction, and that ed schools resisted it for ideological reasons. A recent White House showcase of a humanoid robot teacher gives him a sharp irony: the future of education is a machine doing exactly what teachers were told not to do. He is careful to say sequence matters, not that exploration is bad, and concludes that the answer is a well-trained human who knows the content and how students learn.
points: Teaching is the only knowledge profession that decided its core craft did not need to be taught explicitly.
The case for explicit instruction rests on Rosenshine, Willingham and the science of reading, not on preference.
The author's claim is about sequence: exploration works only after foundational knowledge exists.
Discovery-oriented classrooms mostly benefit students who would have learned anyway, leaving those who most needed instruction behind.
Teachers prepared mainly for facilitation and relationships are vulnerable to replacement by AI delivering instruction, so preparation must teach technique.
quotes: Those things — the actual craft of instruction — were not part of the curriculum. They were, implicitly, beneath it. The ideology of the guide on the side had decided that explicit instruction was a power dynamic to be dismantled rather than a skill to be developed.

Every profession that requires genuine craft teaches the craft explicitly. The practitioner learns the technique — precisely, repeatedly, with feedback — before they earn the right to improvise on it.

Willingham’s work on memory and cognition established that students learn new material by connecting it to things they already know — which requires a teacher who knows what students know and can build the bridge deliberately. Discovery learning assumes the bridge gets built through exploration. The research says it usually doesn’t.

Explicit, systematic phonics instruction works. Balanced literacy — which trusted that children would construct their understanding of how words work through immersion in rich texts — left a generation of students who couldn’t decode.
Cognitive science is clear on this: unguided discovery places a burden on working memory that novice learners cannot carry. They don’t construct understanding. They construct confusion.

But thirty years of evidence has established something the ideology has been reluctant to accept: the students who survive inquiry-based, discovery-oriented classrooms without explicit instruction are almost always the students who were going to learn anyway. Whose background knowledge was rich enough to make the exploration productive. Whose families filled the gap at home.

But here is the uncomfortable thing: we spent thirty years not developing the craft either. We told teachers the relationship was the thing and the instruction would sort itself out. It didn’t. And now we have a technology that does the instruction and a profession that has been prepared primarily for the relationship — which means we have built, with remarkable efficiency, the conditions for our own replacement.
